extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and critics of literature (Coleridge/19th-century literary study)
extracted.subtask_short: literary criticism of poetry and prose
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative criteria and aesthetic judgments found in Coleridge's Table Talk concerning what makes good prose, poetry, illustration, and criticism. Useful for guiding literary appraisal or creative-writing sensibilities for 19th-century English literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful prose — combination of thought, feeling, and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: "The diction is such that it might have been written now, if we could find any one combining so thoughtful a head with so tender a heart and so exquisite a taste."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beautiful prose is marked by the union of intellectual depth (a thoughtful head), emotional sensitivity (a tender heart), and refined aesthetic judgement (exquisite taste). The passage praises Lord Brooke's consolation as exemplifying this combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations should add, not detract; avoid affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Peter Wilkins is to my mind a work of uncommon beauty; and yet Stothard's illustrations have added beauties to it. If it were not for a certain tendency to affectation, scarcely any praise could be too high for Stothard's designs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration can enhance a literary work by adding complementary beauties, but designers/illustrators should avoid affectation. The text gives Stothard as an instance where illustrations increase pleasure but warns that affectation in design undermines praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of composition and perfect plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: "What a master of composition Fielding was!... the Oedipus Tyrannus, the Alchemist, and Tom Jones the three most perfect plots ever planned."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly valued are the structural virtues of composition and plotting—well-planned, cohesive plots are a mark of literary mastery. Fielding is cited as exemplary; comparison with other authors (e.g., Richardson) illustrates how composition affects reader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: charm and wholesomeness over artificial intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: "And how charming, how wholesome, Fielding always is! To take him up after Richardson, is like emerging from a sick room heated by stoves, into an open lawn, on a breezy day in May."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The emotional tone of a work (charming, wholesome) is a criterion; excessive intensity or 'heated' manner (ascribed to Richardson) is presented as less healthful. Tone affects reader comfort and moral/aesthetic reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and sweetness of language as poetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: "[German literary language] was equal to the Greek, except in harmony and sweetness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic language should possess harmony and sweetness; grammatical correctness alone does not guarantee the lyric or melodic qualities that make verse or language feel poetical. Klopstock is used as an example of misapprehending harshness for sweetness by association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic sublimity — not produced by comparative diminution
rubrics_metrics.description: "As to sublimity, he had, with all Germans, one rule for producing it;--it was, to take something very great, and make it very small in comparison with that which you wish to elevate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge (via Coleridge's account) critiques a formulaic device for producing 'sublimity' that relies on diminishing a great object to magnify another; this is presented as an inauthentic or formulaic route to sublimity. Beware mechanical devices that manufacture grandeur by rhetorical trick rather than genuine elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principled criticism to avoid self-contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: "But the Germans were good metaphysicians and critics: they criticised on principles previously laid down; thus, though they might be wrong, they were in no danger of being self-contradictory, which was too often the case with English critics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgment should be grounded in explicit principles. Even if the principles are disputable, applying consistent principles reduces the risk of self-contradiction in criticism. This is offered as a methodological ideal for critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance wit/point with pathos and sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Young... his love of point and wit had often put an end to his pathos and sublimity; but there were parts in him which must be immortal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overemphasis on point, epigram, or wit can undermine deeper emotional or sublime effects in poetry. Writers should balance cleverness with sustaining pathos and grandeur to preserve lasting impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple/commonplace examples to illustrate form
rubrics_metrics.description: "Both [Aristotle and Bacon] wished to confine the attention of the mind in their works to the form of reasoning only, by which other truths might be established or elicited, and therefore the most trite and common-place examples were in fact the best."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For demonstrating logical or formal structures, ordinary or commonplace examples can be virtues: they focus attention on form rather than distract with exotic illustration. This is a defence of plain examples in philosophical or critical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough inquiry into particulars (quid est?)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We had ridiculed their quiddities... had we not borrowed their quantity and their quality, and why then reject their quiddity... every schoolboy in logic must know, that of every thing may be asked, Quantum est? Quale est? and Quid est?... bringing you to the most material of all points, its individual being."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical and philosophical investigation should include careful questioning of particulars ('what is it?'), not shunting aside detailed 'quiddities' as mere pedantry; such inquiry undergirds genuine understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of tone and congruence between plot/machinery and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fault [of the Curse of Kehama]... consisted in the association of a plot and a machinery so very wild with feelings so sober and tender..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mismatch between the extravagance of plot or supernatural machinery and the sobriety/tenderness of feeling can be a defect; successful works align the scale and nature of their plot devices with the emotional register. Conversely, skilful use of exotic elements can be praised when it supports a moral or emotional design (as Coleridge commends in other respects of the poem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral arc and emotional resolution: virtue's triumph must feel credible
rubrics_metrics.description: "...Kehama went on, from the beginning to the end of the poem, increasing in power, whilst Kailyal gradually lost her hopes and her protectors; and, yet by the time we got to the end, we had arrived at an utter contempt and even carelessness of the power of evil, as exemplified in the almighty Rajah, and felt a complete confidence in the safety of the unprotected virtue of the maiden."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's moral architecture—how power and virtue shift across the narrative—should lead readers to a convincing emotional and moral resolution. Coleridge praises a poem that leads readers from fear of evil to confident trust in virtue; such an arc is a mark of artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clarity over compressed concision; avoid corrupt abbreviation
rubrics_metrics.description: "It originated, he thought, in a desire to abbreviate all expression as much as possible... if in one word, without violating idiom, I can express what others have done in more, and yet be as fully and easily understood, I have manifestly made an improvement; but if, on the other hand, it becomes harder, and takes more time to comprehend a thought or image put in one word..., the saving is merely of pen and ink, and the alteration is evidently a corruption."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness is an improvement only when it preserves or enhances clarity and ease of understanding; compression that makes comprehension harder is a corruption of language. This is guidance for word choice and style in composition and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of diction and immutability of word-position in great verse
rubrics_metrics.description: "The excellence of verse, he said, was to be untranslatable into any other words without detriment to the beauty of the passage;--the position of a single word could not be altered in Milton without injury."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excellent poetry often depends on exact diction and the precise placement of words; lines that resist paraphrase without loss are signs of poetic excellence. Poets should attend to the irreplaceability of chosen words and their order.
